opus-5.5.text:
I think the dream is a model that can attend, in a meaningful way, to essentially everything that's relevant to you. Today we have context windows in the millions of tokens, which is already pretty remarkable. You can drop in a whole codebase, a few long books, or hours of video and ask questions about it. But what I'd really like is something that feels like it can attend to trillions of tokens: all of the information on the internet, or all of your personal email, documents, and photos if you've opted in, or every line of code at a large company.

The interesting technical question is that you can't do that with naive quadratic attention. So you need a combination of things: retrieval-style mechanisms that narrow trillions of tokens down to the few million that matter, then a model that reasons deeply over that narrowed set. Ideally, you'd want that whole pipeline to feel seamless and learned end-to-end, rather than a bolted-on search step.

On the capability side, I'd want the model to do real synthesis, not just needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. If you give it a huge software system, it should understand how the pieces fit together, find the subtle bug that spans five files, and propose a change that's consistent with the conventions everywhere else. If you give it a large body of scientific literature, it should notice that a result in one paper contradicts an assumption in another, or that two subfields are working on the same problem under different names.

I'd also want it to be multimodal throughout: long video, audio, sensor data, code, and text all in the same context. A lot of the world's information isn't text, and being able to reason over hours of video as easily as over a document opens up a lot of applications.

And finally, efficiency matters enormously. It's not enough for this to be possible in a research setting. You want it cheap and fast enough that people actually use it day to day. That pushes on everything: model architecture, sparsity, and hardware co-design. That full-stack view is where I think a lot of the progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response describes desired capabilities before discussing technical approaches, but does not advocate defining those capabilities before choosing a solution.

r002.rationale: It says the model should attend to “all of the information on the internet” and discusses asking questions about large context.

r003.rationale: It says trillion-token attention cannot be done with “naive quadratic attention,” motivating retrieval to narrow the context.

r004.rationale: It describes wanting a model that “feels like it can attend to trillions of tokens,” communicating the functional illusion of that scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I keep coming back to is that today, even with a million or two million tokens of context, we're still treating the model like it starts fresh every time. You paste in a bunch of documents, it reasons over them, and then that's gone. What I'd really like is for a model to have essentially all of the context that's relevant to you, all the time, and to be able to attend over it effectively.

Think about what that means concretely. For a software engineer, it's the entire codebase you work on, plus the commit history, plus the design docs, plus the bug reports. Not a retrieval system that pulls in a few chunks it thinks are relevant, but the model actually having the whole thing in its working memory and being able to notice that the function you're about to write duplicates something written three years ago in a different directory. For a researcher, it's every paper you've read, the ones you meant to read, your own notes, your experiment logs. For a doctor, it's a patient's full medical history, not a summary of it.

And then I'd want that context to be personal and persistent. The model should know what you've discussed with it before, what you care about, what you already understand so it doesn't re-explain things, and what you've changed your mind about. Right now we fake that with summaries and memory tricks, and they lose a lot of nuance.

The hard part is that attention over trillions of tokens isn't going to be a naive dense computation. We need something that's more like how the brain works, where most of your memory is dormant and the relevant pieces get activated cheaply when they matter. So I think the interesting research is in the architecture and the systems side: how do you keep that much state around, keep it cheap to serve, and still have the model use it with precision rather than vaguely gesturing at it. If we get that right, the model stops being a very smart stranger and starts being something that actually knows the shape of your problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes desired capabilities before discussing architecture, but it does not advocate defining those capabilities before choosing a technical solution.

r002.rationale: It discusses personal context such as codebases, papers, and medical histories, but does not identify attending to the internet while answering as a desired capability.

r003.rationale: It says attention over trillions of tokens cannot use naive dense computation, but does not identify quadratic scaling as the reason existing attention solutions cannot straightforwardly scale.

r004.rationale: It proposes keeping vast context available while letting relevant memories activate cheaply, describing an effective way to access trillion-token-scale context without dense attention.

astra-6.text:
I’d like them to be able to take in a lot of information and actually use it effectively. Imagine giving a model an entire codebase and asking it to make a change that requires understanding how several different pieces interact. You’d want it to find the relevant pieces, reason about the dependencies, and make a coherent change.

The interesting thing isn’t just how many tokens you can put into the context. It’s whether the model can connect information that’s far apart, recognize what matters for the question you’re asking, and synthesize a useful answer. And ideally that context could include text, images, audio, and video—whatever information is needed to solve the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes useful long-context capabilities and says token count alone is insufficient, but does not advocate defining the goal before choosing a technical solution.

r002.rationale: It discusses finding relevant information in a codebase, but does not identify attending to the internet while answering as a desired capability.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about quadratic scaling or the difficulty of scaling attention to trillion-token contexts.

r004.rationale: It does not propose giving a model the functional illusion of attending to trillions of tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like them to be able to take in all the information that’s relevant to a problem and then actually use it effectively. Imagine being able to give a model a large codebase and ask it to make a change that touches several different parts of the system. It needs to understand how those pieces fit together, rather than just find a function with a similar name.

Or you might have a collection of scientific papers, along with experimental data, and want help figuring out what to try next. The interesting capability isn’t simply fitting all of that into the context window. It’s connecting information across it, noticing inconsistencies, and drawing useful conclusions.

And I’d want that to work across modalities—text, images, audio, video—with reasonable latency and cost. Having a very large context window is useful, but being able to reliably reason over what’s in it is really the goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes desired long-context capabilities, but does not say those should be defined before choosing a technical solution.

r002.rationale: It gives examples involving codebases and scientific papers, but does not identify attending to the internet while answering as a desired capability.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss quadratic scaling or explain why it prevents straightforward scaling to trillion-token contexts.

r004.rationale: It seeks reliable reasoning over large contexts, but does not propose a functional illusion of attending to trillions of tokens.
